archetype.name: Pocket Passer (short-area accuracy)
archetype.definition: A 36-year-old who wins from the pocket with timing and ball placement, throwing short of the sticks and taking his shots selectively, with little left as a runner and a long-running habit of absorbing sacks.

report.headline: Accurate and careful, but 13 deep throws are hiding a sputtering offense
report.take:
Geno Smith is what he has been since his Seattle years: an accurate, rhythm passer whose completion rate (69.4%, 6th) and bad-throw rate (6.8%, 4th) are real skills, not a hot streak. His career says the same. He has posted a top-17 CPOE in four of five full seasons and ranked 1st and 5th in bad-throw rate the last two years. What has changed is the risk profile. After leading the league in interceptions in 2025 with 17, he has none in 147 attempts, and the Jets keep the ball underneath. His average throw is 2.8 yards short of the sticks, and only 13 of 146 charted attempts went 20+ yards.

Those 13 deep throws are carrying the whole season. They produced 3 TDs and 1.93 EPA a play, about 25 points of EPA. His total across 173 dropbacks is only about 9. Take those 13 plays out and the other 160 dropbacks are roughly 16 points below zero. That is the fragile part. A 30.7 CPOE on 13 deep balls will not hold, and the base offense of screens (-0.25 EPA behind the line), checkdowns and third-and-long has been below average. Third down converts at 33% with 8.8 yards to go on average. The red zone sits at -0.42 EPA a play.

The zero interceptions also hide a turnover problem that moved somewhere else. He has 4 turnover-worthy fumbles, 2 of them lost (34th of 43), and a 9.8% sack rate (37th). The sacks are not the price of creating outside the pocket. He scrambles on 5% of dropbacks for 0.03 EPA, and his designed runs lose value. Pressure turns into sacks 38.7% of the time (33rd of 36). That is consistent with his 2025 rate of 46.2% and a Jets line that ranks 26th in allowing hits. It is a trait of this late-career version, not bad luck.

The arc points the wrong way. Weeks 1-3 were efficient: +9.8, +4.3 and +10.9 passing EPA, with Detroit's 31st-ranked defense supplying the 321-yard game. Weeks 4-5 were -4.9 and -11.3, with a 33% bad-throw game in Chicago under 44% pressure. In Week 5 the aDOT collapsed to 5.0 against Cleveland. Now he loses his best per-target receiver (Mitchell), a starting guard (Parham) and Breece Hall, and may lose his tight end (Sadiq). Expect a careful, sack-prone game manager with occasional deep strikes. That is a QB who keeps the Jets close more than one who wins games for them.

strengths.title: Accuracy that has held for years
strengths.body: His 69.4% completion rate ranks 6th, and charting has him missing his spot only 6.8% of the time. This is the stable core of his game. He was top-8 in completion percentage in 2022 and 2024 and 1st in bad-throw rate in 2024. It should last even as the supporting cast thins.

strengths.title: Deep shots when he takes them
strengths.body: On 13 throws of 20+ air yards he has 3 TDs, no picks and 1.93 EPA a play, much of it to Garrett Wilson (0.455 EPA per target on a team-high 43 looks). The skill is real: he picks his moments and places the ball. The rate is not, because a 30.7 CPOE on 13 attempts is a hot streak. Expect the deep shots to keep coming, just less efficiently.

strengths.title: Interception avoidance (for now)
strengths.body: Zero picks in 147 attempts ranks 1st, helped by a conservative 6.9-yard intended depth and a scheme that keeps him short of the sticks. His history says this is partly a sample. He threw 15 and 17 interceptions the last two seasons. The safer throw profile should keep his rate below his 2025 level, but not at zero.

concerns.title: Sacks and fumbles replace interceptions
concerns.body: A 9.8% sack rate and a 38.7% pressure-to-sack rate are near the bottom of the league. He also has 4 turnover-worthy fumbles, 2 lost. He isn't buying time to make plays: his scrambles barely break even. This matches his 2025 profile, and with guard Dylan Parham out behind a line that ranks 26th in allowing hits, it is not getting fixed soon.

concerns.title: The base offense is below water
concerns.body: Outside the deep shots, the down-to-down offense is bad. Screens and throws behind the line run at -0.25 EPA, third down converts at 33% with long distances, and red-zone dropbacks sit at -0.42 EPA. These are situations the Jets' conservative, underneath design is supposed to win, and it isn't. That points to a cast and line problem more than to him.

concerns.title: Recent form and a thinning cast
concerns.body: His last two games produced a combined -16.2 passing EPA, with 44% pressure and a 33% bad-throw rate in Chicago and a 5.0 aDOT against Cleveland. Adonai Mitchell (0.576 EPA per target) and Breece Hall are out, and Kenyon Sadiq is in concussion protocol. That pushes even more volume onto Wilson and lower-value options.

trend.note: Three efficient starts, peaking at +10.9 EPA against Detroit's 31st-ranked defense, gave way to back-to-back negative games against Chicago and Cleveland. His depth of target shrank and the sacks stayed at 3-5 a game.

nextGame.headline: A depleted Patriots secondary versus a depleted Jets offense
nextGame.body:
On paper New England's pass defense is a problem: 5th in EPA allowed per dropback, 7th in success rate, and stingy against tight ends (TE1s 5.1 PPR under their averages, 2nd). The seams are deep and underneath. The Patriots rank 24th in deep EPA allowed, which is exactly where Smith has made his season, and as 7.5-point road dogs the Jets should be throwing late. New England's pass rush is ordinary (15th in sack rate), less than what he faced in Chicago, but his own sack habit doesn't need much help.

Availability tilts this more than the season numbers. New England is without both starting corners, Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III (95% of snaps each), plus two depth corners, and Charles Woods is questionable. That is a backup-heavy secondary facing Garrett Wilson, and it weakens the 5th-ranked pass defense and the 8th-ranked WR1 coverage. On the Jets' side, Mitchell, Hall and guard Parham are out and Sadiq is questionable, so the target tree narrows to Wilson, Isaiah Williams and Braelon Allen, whose targets have been negative EPA. Dre'Mont Jones (questionable) matters for the Patriots' rush. The early forecast has 12 mph wind with gusts near 19: worth watching for the deep ball, not yet a reason to change the read.

keyMatchups.title: Wilson against backup corners
keyMatchups.body: Wilson has absorbed 43 targets at 0.455 EPA each. With Gonzalez and Davis both out, New England has to cover him with its depth chart. This is the cleanest path to Smith's production, and with Mitchell out the ball should funnel there even more.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a soft spot
keyMatchups.body: New England allows 0.843 EPA on deep throws (24th), and Smith's 13 deep attempts have carried his season. If the wind stays manageable and protection holds for 2.9 seconds, this is where the Jets can steal points. If the shots don't land, his underneath game hasn't been good enough to sustain drives.

keyMatchups.title: Run the ball at a 30th-ranked front
keyMatchups.body: New England is 30th in rush EPA allowed. A Jets ground game that can stay on schedule, even without Hall, is the best protection for a QB who takes a sack on nearly 10% of dropbacks. Game script works against it, though, if the Patriots' 9th-ranked pass offense jumps ahead.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Jets keep taking downfield shots at New England's backup corners, or retreat to the 5-yard aDOT and sack-heavy dropbacks they used against Cleveland.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy and the underneath approach are sustainable. His completion rate and bad-throw rate match three seasons of evidence, and the Jets' design keeps throws short. Two numbers will regress. The deep-ball efficiency (1.93 EPA a play on 13 attempts) will cool, and the zero interceptions will not survive a full season for a QB who threw 32 picks over the previous two years, though the conservative depth should keep him under his 2025 pace. The sack rate is not regression material. It is his recent norm behind a weak line, and the fumbles come with it.

That makes him a low-ceiling starter. Expect roughly 200-230 passing yards and 1-1.5 TDs a game, about three sacks, and an interception every other game or so, with almost no rushing value. The team outlook depends on the health of the receivers and line more than on him. When Mitchell, Hall and Parham return, the base offense should climb back toward neutral. Until then he is a QB who keeps games close rather than one who wins shootouts.
swingFactors: Return of Mitchell, Hall and guard Parham
Whether the deep-ball hit rate holds up
Pass protection and his pressure-to-sack habit

bets.reason: His 0 interceptions in 147 attempts runs against a career that included a league-worst 17 picks in 2025. As a 7.5-point road dog he should be throwing late into a pass defense ranked 5th in EPA. Backup corners can be beaten, but they can also be baited.

He has taken 3-5 sacks in each of the last four games with a 38.7% pressure-to-sack rate (33rd of 36). Guard Parham is out and the Jets rank 26th in allowing hits. Trailing should produce more dropbacks against a middling New England rush.

The Jets are 3-1-1 against the spread with a 7th-ranked defense and the 2nd-best sack rate. New England is missing both starting corners and may lose OT Will Campbell and TreVeyon Henderson. Smith's low-turnover, short game tends to keep scores tight even when the offense stalls.

Four of five Jets games went under. Their offense ranks 20th and is missing Mitchell, Hall and Parham, and their defense ranks 7th. New England's 45-point game against the Raiders and its strong pass offense keep this a modest lean.

confidence.note: Five games, with the season's value concentrated in 13 deep throws. The career profile is stable, but the Jets' injury list changes the cast this week.
